[Supreme Court]{.status .status-case} [299 U.S. 304](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-299/pdf/USREPORTS-299-304.pdf){.cite} [Decided December 21, 1936]{.cite} [7 to 1]{.cite}

**Holding.** Upheld the delegation. Because foreign affairs powers rest on national sovereignty rather than on the Constitution's specific grants alone, Congress may give the President broader discretion abroad than at home.

**Question.** Whether a 1934 joint resolution letting the President ban arms sales to the countries fighting the Chaco War, Bolivia and Paraguay, was an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the opinion** (official text)

[Opinion: 299 U.S. 304](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-299/pdf/USREPORTS-299-304.pdf){.btn-official}
:::

Background reading: [Wikipedia article on Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Curtiss-Wright_Export_Corp.) (secondary source).

## Why it matters

The most cited case for executive power in foreign affairs, chiefly for Justice Sutherland's description of the President as the "sole organ of the federal government in the field of international relations." That language was not needed to decide the case, and executive branch lawyers have long relied on it. Its delegation holding underpins the broad discretion Congress grants in statutes such as the [IEEPA](../statutes/ieepa-1977.qmd) and the [Arms Export Control Act](../statutes/aeca-1976.qmd).

## Status

The delegation holding remains good law. In [Zivotofsky v. Kerry](../cases/zivotofsky-2015.qmd) the Court declined to read the "sole organ" language as establishing exclusive presidential power in foreign affairs.

## Statutes at issue

- [Constitution (war powers)](../statutes/constitution-war-powers.qmd){.subj}. Treated the foreign affairs power as an attribute of national sovereignty, supporting broad delegations to the President.

Studied in [Unit 1: Where the power comes from](../study/units/foundations.qmd).
